entries.task_prompt: Hey, before I touch anything, can you give the database a quick health check? I just want to know it's behaving normally. After that, I'd like you to spin up a tiny staging area called agenticmcpe_bench_courier — a fresh schema with one table in it called dispatches. Give it an id (integer primary key, auto-incrementing), a status column that only allows 'pending', 'in_transit', or 'delivered', an origin (text), a destination (text), and a weight_kg (numeric). Then seed it with these five rows exactly: (1, 'delivered',    'Berlin',     'Paris',     2.5), (2, 'in_transit',  'Lisbon',     'Madrid',    0.8), (3, 'pending',     'Tokyo',      'Osaka',     12.0), (4, 'delivered',   'Cape Town',  'Nairobi',   4.2), (5, 'in_transit',  'Toronto',    'Montreal',  1.1). Once they're in, please read the table back ordered by id so I can eyeball that everything landed correctly.

Then insert the following six rows verbatim, in this exact order, with all values matching exactly: (default, 'sev1', 'api-gateway', true, 12), (default, 'sev2', 'auth-service', true, 27), (default, 'sev3', 'billing-worker', false, 45), (default, 'sev1', 'search-indexer', true, 8), (default, 'sev2', 'api-gateway', false, 60), (default, 'sev3', 'notifications', true, 15). entries.task_prompt:
Hey, I fat-fingered a destination city in a seed load and want to patch it in a clean little sandbox so nothing outside gets touched. Can you set up a schema called `agenticmcpe_bench_logistics` and inside it build a `shipments` table with columns: id serial primary key, tracking_no text, carrier text, status text with a CHECK that status is one of ('pending','in_transit','delivered','returned'), and destination text.

Then load these exact four rows in order:

  (1, 'TRK-001', 'DHL',   'delivered',   'Berlin')
  (2, 'TRK-002', 'UPS',   'in_transit',  'Hamberg')
  (3, 'TRK-003', 'FedEx', 'pending',     'Madrid')
  (4, 'TRK-004', 'DPD',   'returned',    'Dublin')

Row 2 is the one I typoed — the city got typed as 'Hamberg' but it should be 'Hamburg'. Please update the row where id = 2 and set destination to the literal 'Hamburg' (no string tricks, just an absolute assignment). After that's done, show me the full table ordered by id so I can eyeball the corrected city.

While you're at it, give me a quick read on the table shape (list the objects in the new schema and pull the column detail for shipments) and finish with the standard database health check so I can see we're still in good shape after the patch.

entries.task_prompt: I'm prepping for a deploy on a PostgreSQL database I haven't worked with much, and I want to understand how the planner handles a simple lookup against the system catalog pg_class before I trust it for an inventory job. Could you walk me through this end to end? First, list the schemas in the database and confirm that pg_catalog is there. Then list the objects inside pg_catalog so I can see pg_class exists, and pull up the column details for pg_class so I know exactly which columns I'm selecting. Once that's grounded, run plain EXPLAIN (not ANALYZE) on a SELECT that pulls relname and relkind from pg_catalog.pg_class with no WHERE clause, then run EXPLAIN again on the same SELECT but with a WHERE relkind = 'r' clause so I can compare the two plan shapes side by side. After that, run one more EXPLAIN on the same SELECT but with both a relkind = 'r' filter and a relname LIKE 'pg_%' filter, so I can see how an additional predicate changes the plan. While you're at it, also do a standard database health check so I know if there are any planner-related warnings I should be aware of. Finally, just as a sanity check, run a real SELECT against pg_class pulling relname and relkind for the first ten rows so I can see actual values the plans would be touching. Don't run ANALYZE — I only want to see the plan shapes. This is purely read-only; do not create or modify anything.

entries.task_prompt: I'm sketching the schema for a small widget catalogue ahead of a feature rollout and I want to walk through a realistic table-evolution. Please set up a fresh dedicated schema called agenticmcpe_bench_widget_catalogue and inside it create a widgets table with an id serial primary key, a sku text, a name text, and a price_cents integer. Seed it with exactly these three rows: (1, 'WID-A', 'Alpha widget', 1999), (2, 'WID-B', 'Bravo widget', 4599), and (3, 'WID-C', 'Charlie widget', 899). Then evolve the table by ALTERing it to add a new weight_grams integer column that is NOT NULL with a default of 0. After that, backfill that column with an absolute update so the rows end up at exactly: WID-A -> 120, WID-B -> 340, and WID-C -> 55. Finally, confirm the end state by listing the objects in the new schema, fetching the column details for the widgets table, and selecting all rows from widgets ordered by id so I can see the new column with the backfilled values.

entries.task_prompt: Before I sign off on the staging cutover I want a thorough but fully read-only health sweep of this PostgreSQL instance — no DDL, no DML, just inspection. Run the standard database health check so I can see which components (index, connection, vacuum, sequence, replication, buffer, constraint) raise any flags. SELECT

  (ARRAY['10.0.0.5','10.0.0.17','10.0.0.42','192.168.1.3','192.168.1.8','172.16.0.9','203.0.113.4','198.51.100.7'])[1 + (g % 8)] AS source_ip,

entries.task_prompt: I'm auditing an unfamiliar PostgreSQL instance and need a quick read-only orientation. Could you pull a consolidated snapshot: start by listing the schemas and the contents of information_schema so I can see what metadata tables/views it exposes, then capture installed extensions with their installed and default versions, and read max_connections, shared_buffers, and work_mem from pg_settings. After that, check whether the server is in recovery (primary vs replica), pull replica count from pg_stat_replication if it is a primary, run the connection-focused health check, and finally compute the current session count from pg_stat_activity next to max_connections so I can see the headroom. Nothing should be written.

No writes occur at any step.

thinking: First I list the schemas in the database to know what's available, especially which contain user objects versus system schemas.

Then I list the objects in information_schema so I can see which tables/views/sequences it actually exposes — information_schema has dozens of entries and I want to confirm what's there before drilling in.
Next I check installed extensions via pg_extension joined with pg_available_extensions to get installed_version AND default_version side by side, ordered by extname.
Then I read pg_settings for max_connections so I know the configured connection ceiling.
I also read shared_buffers from pg_settings to understand current memory configuration.
And work_mem from pg_settings too — three memory/connection settings in one focused look.
I run analyze_db_health for the connection component specifically to see if there's any concern about current connection pressure vs max_connections.
Then I check pg_is_in_recovery() to determine if this instance is a primary or standby, and conditionally read pg_stat_replication to count connected replicas when primary.
Finally I issue a SELECT count(*) on pg_stat_activity to get the actual current session count so I can compare it against max_connections for a concrete headroom number in a single SQL expression.

entries.task_prompt: Hey, I'm poking at an unfamiliar Postgres instance and want to get a feel for how the planner treats filtered versus unfiltered queries against the system catalogs. Could you start by listing the schemas so I can see what's available, then run EXPLAIN (plain plan, no ANALYZE) on a SELECT against pg_class that just groups rows by relkind without any filter? After that, run the same shape of SELECT but with a WHERE relkind='r' filter before the GROUP BY so I can compare the two plans side by side. I'd also like to see the detailed column metadata for pg_class so I understand the data types the planner is working with, and pull a couple of pg_settings values (random_page_cost and seq_page_cost) that factor into the cost estimates. Finally, run one more EXPLAIN pair — this time joining pg_class to pg_index and grouping by relkind, again once unfiltered and once filtered to relkind='r' — and wrap up with a quick SELECT that shows the actual count of rows per relkind in pg_class so the plans have real numbers to compare against. This is purely read-only, nothing should be modified.

entries.task_prompt: Hi! I'm trying to get comfortable with how Postgres hands out sequence-backed ids and would love a small worked example I can replay. Could you set up a fresh schema called `agenticmcpe_bench_quiz_counter` (please keep everything in there — don't touch public) and inside it first create an explicit sequence called `quiz_attempts_id_seq` so it's a real visible object? Then build a `quiz_attempts` table with an integer `id` primary key that defaults to nextval from that sequence, a `topic` text NOT NULL column, and a `score` integer column with a CHECK that score is >= 0. After the table exists, insert 4 rows for me — don't pass the id, let Postgres fill it in — using these exact (topic, score) values: ('algebra', 85), ('geometry', 72), ('calculus', 91), ('statistics', 68). Then read the rows back ordered by id ascending so I can see which numbers got assigned, give me a quick summary line with the highest id assigned and the total row count, and finally list the objects in the schema so I can confirm both the table and the sequence are actually there. Thanks!

entries.task_prompt: Pre-deploy perf sanity for our new order-archive screen. I'm worried a lookup like `WHERE region = $1 AND customer_id = $2 ORDER BY placed_on DESC` is going to turn into the next hot path in pg_stat_statements, so please spin up a representative working table called `agenticmcpe_bench_order_archive` in the public schema with columns id serial PRIMARY KEY, customer_id int, region text, total_cents int, placed_on date. Bulk-seed it with about 3500 rows in a single INSERT ... SELECT generate_series(1,3500) statement (cycle customer_id across 1..50 and region across 'north','south','east','west' so filter selectivity is realistic) and then ANALYZE it so the planner sees something real. Next, run the index advisor on two concrete queries against that table (referenced unqualified): one filtering on region and customer_id and ordering by placed_on DESC, and one that just counts rows for a given customer_id. CREATE whatever indexes the advisor recommends, re-ANALYZE the table, and EXPLAIN the filtered+ordered lookup again so I can see the planner actually picks up the new index instead of falling back to a seq scan. Finally, list the indexes on the table to confirm the recommended one is registered. Nothing else — table stays in public, no other schemas.

arguments.sql:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS public.agenticmcpe_bench_order_archive (
  id serial PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id int,
  region text,
  total_cents int,
  placed_on date
);

steps.description: Create the working table in public schema with the required columns (id serial PK, customer_id int, region text, total_cents int, placed_on date).

arguments.sql:
INSERT INTO public.agenticmcpe_bench_order_archive (customer_id, region, total_cents, placed_on)
SELECT
  ((g - 1) % 50) + 1                                  AS customer_id,
  CASE ((g - 1) % 4)
    WHEN 0 THEN 'north'
    WHEN 1 THEN 'south'
    WHEN 2 THEN 'east'
    ELSE        'west'
  END                                                  AS region,
  ((g * 137) % 99000) + 1000                           AS total_cents,
  (date '2023-01-01' + ((g - 1) % 365))                AS placed_on
FROM generate_series(1, 3500) AS g;

post_action_properties.metamorphic: public.agenticmcpe_bench_order_archive now holds exactly 3500 rows with customer_id cycling 1..50 and region cycling north/south/east/west

entries.task_prompt:
Hey, I'm trying to get a feel for how Postgres plans queries against its own catalogs. Could you run a small read-only investigation for me?

Start by listing the schemas in the database so I can see what's there. Then I want four EXPLAIN (no ANALYZE, just plans) variants run against pg_class so I can compare them side by side:
1. A plain count of all rows in pg_class — no filter at all.
2. The same count but filtered to relkind = 'r' (ordinary tables).
3. The filtered count again, this time joined to pg_index on pg_class.oid = pg_index.indrelid.
4. (Optional but nice) The unfiltered count joined to pg_index.

While you're at it, please also pull the column metadata for pg_class so I know what fields it actually has, read random_page_cost and seq_page_cost from pg_settings (those matter for the plan interpretation), and finish with a SELECT that groups pg_class by relkind and returns the row counts — that way the plans have real numbers to compare against.

Everything read-only, please — no DDL, no DML. Just the plans and the supporting context.
entries.task_summary: Read-only investigation of how Postgres plans queries against its own catalogs. First lists schemas, then runs four EXPLAIN (no ANALYZE) variants against pg_class (unfiltered count, filtered count on relkind='r', filtered count joined to pg_index, unfiltered count joined to pg_index). Also retrieves pg_class column metadata via get_object_details, reads random_page_cost and seq_page_cost from pg_settings, and finishes with a SELECT that groups pg_class by relkind to provide real row-count numbers to compare against the plans.

arguments.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_catalog.pg_class

post_action_properties.metamorphic: explain output references an Aggregate node on top of a Seq Scan (or Index Only Scan) over pg_class with no filter

steps.description: EXPLAIN variant 1: a plain count(*) over all rows of pg_class, no filter. Baseline plan with no selectivity.

post_action_properties.metamorphic: explain output includes a Filter (relkind = 'r') on the pg_class scan node

post_action_properties.metamorphic: explain output contains a join node referencing both pg_class and pg_index without a Filter on relkind

steps.description: EXPLAIN variant 4: unfiltered count joined to pg_index. Same shape as variant 3 but without the relkind predicate, so we can see the planner's choice change.

post_action_properties.metamorphic: result rows cover relkind values including 'r' and at least one other, so the plans have real per-kind counts to compare against

steps.description: Final supporting read: GROUP pg_class by relkind and return row counts. Gives the user concrete numbers — especially the relkind='r' count and total — to correlate with the EXPLAIN estimates.

thinking: First, orient by listing all schemas so I know what's in the database.
Then run EXPLAIN (without ANALYZE) on a SELECT that counts all rows in pg_class with no filter — this shows the planner's baseline cost for a sequential scan over the catalog.
Next, run EXPLAIN on a filtered variant that counts rows in pg_class where relkind = 'r' (ordinary tables) — this shows how the planner treats a simple equality filter on relkind.
Then run EXPLAIN on a JOIN of pg_class to pg_index on pg_class.oid = pg_index.indrelid, again filtered to relkind = 'r', to see how the planner handles a catalog join.
Pull the column metadata for pg_class from information_schema.columns (or pg_attribute) so we know what columns exist and their types.
Read two pg_settings values: random_page_cost and seq_page_cost, since these directly influence the planner's choice between seq scan and index scan — relevant context for interpreting the plans.
Run a final read-only aggregation: SELECT relkind, COUNT(*) FROM pg_class GROUP BY relkind ORDER BY 2 DESC, so the plans have actual row numbers to compare against.
Summarize the comparison by stating the planner's chosen node types and estimated row counts for each of the four EXPLAIN variants.

1. Create a fresh schema called `agenticmcpe_bench_feedback_digest` (lowercase snake_case). All writes for this task go inside it — please don't touch `public` or any other schema.

2. Inside that schema, create a table named `feedback` with these columns:
   - `feedback_id` integer, PRIMARY KEY
   - `category` text, NOT NULL
   - `rating` integer, NOT NULL
   - `comment` text

   Then insert exactly these 7 rows (verbatim, in this order):
   (1, 'app',     5, 'love the new dashboard')
   (2, 'app',     4, 'crashes on mobile sometimes')
   (3, 'app',     3, 'okay overall')
   (4, 'support', 2, 'slow reply last time')
   (5, 'support', 4, 'agent was helpful')
   (6, 'app',     5, 'smooth experience')
   (7, 'support', 1, 'unresolved issue')

3. Create a view `feedback_app_summary` over `feedback` that filters rows where `category = 'app'` and returns a single summary row with three columns:
   - `category` — the literal string 'app'
   - `feedback_count` — COUNT(*) of the filtered rows (should be 4)
   - `avg_rating` — AVG(rating)::numeric(10,2) over the filtered rows (should be 4.25)

   Both the filter and the aggregates need to be expressed inside the view's single CREATE VIEW statement.

4. Run a SELECT against `agenticmcpe_bench_feedback_digest.feedback_app_summary` so I can see the report row, then list the objects in that schema to confirm both `feedback` (table) and `feedback_app_summary` (view) are registered.

That's it — stop after the last verification step.

entries.task_prompt:
I'm joining a new team and want to do a quick health-audit pass on our shared Postgres instance before I start running my own workload against it — basically get oriented on whether there are any obvious warning signs in the indexes and connections areas, and grab a couple of related facts from the system catalogs.

Concretely, please:

1. Run the built-in database health check scoped to the `index` component so I can see if there are any bloat, missing-index, or unused-index warnings.

2. Run the same built-in database health check, this time scoped to the `connection` component, so I can see current vs. max connection usage and any connection-related flags.

3. Pull `max_connections` and `superuser_reserved_connections` from `pg_settings` (I want the setting value and the `pending_restart` column) so I can cross-check what the connection health check reported.

4. Finish with a single read-only line that returns `current_database()`, `current_user`, and `version()` on one row, just so the audit note has a clean identity stamp at the bottom.

Everything must be read-only — no DDL, no DML, no schema writes. Just the health-check output and the supporting catalog facts.

entries.task_prompt:
Hey, I'm putting together a small lookup table for a bookstore catalog feature and I'd like to make a single-ISBN lookup fast. Could you set everything up in a fresh schema called `agenticmcpe_bench_bookshelve_lookup` (please create it yourself — that's the only place anything should be written).

Inside that schema, create a table `books` with these columns:
- `id` serial PRIMARY KEY
- `isbn` text NOT NULL
- `title` text NOT NULL
- `genre` text NOT NULL

Then bulk-seed exactly these eight rows in this order (let Postgres fill the id):

('978-0143124870', 'The Midnight Library', 'fiction')
('978-0525559474', 'The Vanishing Half', 'fiction')
('978-0062316097', 'Sapiens', 'history')
('978-0553109435', 'A Brief History of Time', 'science')
('978-0747532699', 'Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone', 'fantasy')
('978-0261103573', 'The Hobbit', 'fantasy')
('978-0385472579', 'The Alienist', 'mystery')
('978-0451524935', '1984', 'dystopia')

Once the data is loaded, run EXPLAIN (no ANALYZE) on `SELECT * FROM agenticmcpe_bench_bookshelve_lookup.books WHERE isbn = '978-0747532699'` so I can see the baseline plan. After that, create an index called `idx_books_isbn` on the `isbn` column. Then re-run EXPLAIN on the exact same lookup so I can compare the plans side by side, and finally pull the detailed structure of the `books` table so I can verify the index is registered and see its definition. Nothing should be created outside of `agenticmcpe_bench_bookshelve_lookup`.

entries.task_prompt:
Hey, I need to stage a small data migration: pull a subset of rows out of one table into a sibling archive table inside their own dedicated schema, then clean up the source. Please set everything up from scratch — nothing pre-existing should be touched.

Create a fresh schema called `agenticmcpe_bench_ticket_archive_split`. Inside it, build two tables with the same shape:

`tickets` (source) and `tickets_archived` (destination), both with:
- `id` serial PRIMARY KEY
- `customer_id` text NOT NULL
- `priority` text NOT NULL
- `status` text NOT NULL
- `created_year` integer NOT NULL

Bulk-seed `tickets` with exactly these eight rows in this order (let Postgres fill the id):

('C-101', 'high',   'open',     2024)
('C-102', 'high',   'closed',   2024)
('C-103', 'high',   'open',     2025)
('C-201', 'medium', 'open',     2024)
('C-202', 'low',    'closed',   2023)
('C-301', 'high',   'open',     2025)
('C-302', 'medium', 'pending',  2024)
('C-303', 'low',    'open',     2025)

The qualifying subset is `priority = 'high' AND status = 'open'` — from the seed above that should be exactly three rows. The migration is: copy those three into `tickets_archived`, then delete them from `tickets`.

Concretely I'd like you to:
1. Show the BEFORE view: the qualifying rows from `tickets` ordered by id.
2. Run an INSERT ... SELECT into `tickets_archived` for that subset.
3. Show the AFTER view: the rows now in `tickets_archived` ordered by id.
4. DELETE the qualifying rows from `tickets`.
5. Confirm the source no longer contains any qualifying rows, and report the final row counts for both tables (tickets should end up at 5, tickets_archived at 3).
6. List the schema's objects so I can see both tables are registered.

Everything write-related has to live inside `agenticmcpe_bench_ticket_archive_split`. Nothing should be created or modified anywhere else.

entries.task_prompt:
Hi! I'd like a read-only orientation audit of this Postgres instance since I'm new to it. No DDL or DML, please; just inspections against the system catalogs and built-in health checks.

Concretely I need:

1. A list of every schema in the database so I can see the layout.
2. Full column and constraint metadata for `pg_catalog.pg_class` so I know what fields it exposes.
3. The set of installed extensions with their installed version and the corresponding default version from `pg_available_extensions`, ordered by extension name.
4. A one-line identity stamp combining `current_database()`, `current_user`, and `version()`.
5. The current `random_page_cost` and `seq_page_cost` values from `pg_settings` (I want name, setting, unit, category so I can sanity-check planner costing).
6. `max_connections` and `superuser_reserved_connections` from `pg_settings`, including the `pending_restart` flag for each, so I can tell whether a restart is queued after config changes.
7. A table count per non-system schema derived from `information_schema.tables`, grouped by `table_schema` and ordered by count descending then schema name ascending — this gives me a quick sense of where the data lives.
8. The built-in database health check scoped to the `connection` component, cross-checked against the settings pulled in step 6.
9. The built-in database health check scoped to the `index` component to round out the audit.

All steps are pure reads. Please don't create or modify anything.

entries.task_prompt:
I'm chasing a slow badge-lookup on a visitor log table and I want to prove the tuning advisor can fix it. Please do this on our shared Postgres instance:

1. Create a working table called `agenticmcpe_bench_visit_log` directly in the public schema with these columns: `id` SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, `visitor_name` text NOT NULL, `badge_no` text NOT NULL, `purpose` text NOT NULL, and `checked_in_at` timestamp NOT NULL DEFAULT '2025-01-01 09:00:00'.

2. Bulk-seed it with 3000 rows in a single INSERT ... SELECT generate_series(...) statement. Spread the values across a handful of fixed visitor_names, badge_no values like 'BP-1001' through 'BP-1005', and purposes such as 'tour', 'delivery', 'interview', 'vendor'. Just make sure every row is well-formed.

3. Run ANALYZE on `agenticmcpe_bench_visit_log` so the planner sees fresh stats.

4. Ask the index advisor to analyze this concrete query against the working table (referenced unqualified, just `agenticmcpe_bench_visit_log`):
   SELECT * FROM agenticmcpe_bench_visit_log WHERE badge_no = 'BP-1003';

5. Create the index the advisor recommends.

6. Verify the new index exists on `agenticmcpe_bench_visit_log` by listing its indexes from pg_indexes, and confirm via EXPLAIN (no ANALYZE) that the lookup plan now uses that index.

entries.task_prompt: Hi — I'm doing a quick orientation audit on this Postgres instance and I'd like a single concrete answer about what extensions are actually installed and at which versions, plus a one-line identity stamp so I know which database and user I'm talking to. Please run one read-only SELECT that returns, for every row of pg_extension, the extension name and its extversion, alongside the current_database(), current_user, and server_version (cast to text) so I can see them on the same result. Then, in a second read-only SELECT, give me a side-by-side comparison of installed versus available extensions by joining pg_extension against pg_available_extensions on name, showing installed_extension_name, installed_version, default_version, and installed (a boolean that is true when the extension is loaded and false when it is merely available). Please don't change anything — pure reads.
entries.task_summary: Two read-only SELECTs: (1) list every row of pg_extension with name and extversion alongside current_database(), current_user, and server_version::text; (2) join pg_extension against pg_available_extensions on name to compare installed vs available extensions, returning installed_extension_name, installed_version, default_version, and installed (true if loaded in pg_extension, false if only available).

arguments.sql: SELECT e.extname AS extension_name, e.extversion AS installed_version, current_database() AS current_database, current_user AS current_user, (SELECT setting FROM pg_settings WHERE name = 'server_version') AS server_version FROM pg_extension e ORDER BY e.extname

steps.description: Single read-only SELECT returning one row per installed extension in pg_extension (extname, extversion) together with the identity stamp current_database(), current_user, and server_version (selected from pg_settings and cast to text). No DDL/DML — pure read.

arguments.sql: SELECT ae.name AS installed_extension_name, e.extversion AS installed_version, ae.default_version AS default_version, (e.extname IS NOT NULL) AS installed FROM pg_available_extensions ae LEFT JOIN pg_extension e ON e.extname = ae.name ORDER BY ae.name

steps.description: Read-only SELECT joining pg_available_extensions (alias ae) to pg_extension (alias e) on name via LEFT JOIN so every available extension appears; installed is true only when the extension is actually loaded into pg_extension. Pure read.

This is one execute_sql call returning multiple rows (one per extension) plus the identity stamp repeated. No DDL, no DML.

Step 2: Sanity-check the answer with a second read-only call that lists installed vs available extensions side by side via pg_available_extensions joined to pg_extension, so the analyst sees what is loaded and what else could be turned on. This is a second execute_sql call.

entries.task_prompt: Hey, before we greenlight this morning's deploy I want a thorough pre-flight health snapshot of our Postgres instance — purely read-only, nothing gets created or modified. Can you run the built-in health analysis four times, once for each of these components: 'index', 'connection', 'vacuum', and 'replication'. After that, please pull a few cross-checks straight from the catalogs: the current value of `max_connections` from `pg_settings`, the current value of `autovacuum` from `pg_settings`, and a single aggregate query over `pg_stat_user_tables` that sums `n_dead_tup` across user tables so I can see total bloat pressure at a glance. Then throw in a one-line identity stamp with `current_database`, `current_user`, and `server_version`. On top of all that, please also grab the top queries by total time from `pg_stat_statements` and finish with a workload-wide index advisor run, so I can compare any index recommendations against the 'index' health check. No DDL, no DML — just reads and the health tool — and I want everything in one clean report.
entries.task_summary: Read-only pre-flight health snapshot of the Postgres instance: runs the built-in health tool four times (index, connection, vacuum, replication), pulls three single-row catalog cross-checks (max_connections, autovacuum, sum(n_dead_tup) over pg_stat_user_tables), prints a one-line identity stamp (current_database, current_user, server_version), grabs the top queries by total time from pg_stat_statements, and finishes with a workload-wide index advisor run. All eight reads run in parallel where possible; only execute_sql is used for the four catalog selects and the identity stamp.

entries.task_prompt: Doing a quick perf sanity check on the Postgres instance before today's deploy and I'd like a fuller picture than usual. First, pull the top queries out of pg_stat_statements twice — once sorted by total time so I can see where cumulative cost has piled up, and once sorted by mean time so the occasional expensive calls don't drown out the per-call hot ones. While you're there, run the built-in health check for both the connection and index components so I know saturation and index bloat in the same pass. Then grab two planner-cost knobs from pg_settings — random_page_cost and effective_cache_size — in a single SELECT with simple aliases so the values are easy to read. After that, ask the workload-wide index advisor what it would recommend for the recorded workload. Finish with a one-line identity stamp (current_database, current_user, server_version) so I can pin the report to a specific instance, and as a last touch, EXPLAIN (no ANALYZE, no BUFFERS) the literal query SELECT * FROM pg_catalog.pg_stat_database so I can see the planner's chosen scan strategy for that catalog. entries.task_prompt:
Hey, I'm staging a small migration on a synthetic event stream and want to validate two different index shapes against a moderately sized table before I commit to the design. Could you set up a fresh, dedicated schema called agenticmcpe_bench_event_stream so the experiment is fully isolated, and inside it build a table called event_log with an id (bigint, primary key), a region text column (not null), an event_type text column (not null), a payload text column, and a created_at timestamp column?

Once the table exists, please bulk-seed it with a few thousand rows in a single INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM generate_series(...) statement so the indexes have something realistic to operate on — pick whatever mix of region, event_type, payload, and created_at values you like as long as it's one statement — and then run ANALYZE on event_log afterwards so the planner has fresh stats.

Then I want you to create TWO different indexes on event_log: (1) a plain btree index on the region column for the common region-scoped lookups, and (2) a partial btree index on event_type restricted to rows where event_type = 'error', since error queries are a hot path and I want that index lean. After both are in place, please confirm both indexes actually exist by querying the catalog in a single SELECT — give me the index name, the indexed column/expression, and any predicate so I can see both shapes side by side. Nothing fancy beyond that, I just want the two index flavors landed and visible.

SELECT ... FROM generate_series(...) with a realistic mix, ANALYZE it, then create two indexes: a plain btree on region and a partial btree on event_type WHERE event_type = 'error'. Finish with one catalog SELECT that returns index name, indexed column/expression, and any predicate for both indexes side by side.

  (ARRAY['click','view','error','login','signup','purchase'])[1 + (g % 6)],
  'payload-' || g || '-' || md5(g::text),
  '2024-01-01 00:00:00'::timestamp + (g * interval '1 minute')
FROM generate_series(1, 5000) AS g
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING

arguments.sql:
SELECT
  i.indexname AS index_name,
  i.indexdef AS index_def,
  pg_get_indexdef(c.oid, (SELECT array_position(ix.indkey::int[], k.attnum)), true) AS indexed_column_or_expression,
  pg_get_expr(ix.indpred, ix.indrelid) AS predicate
FROM pg_indexes i
JOIN pg_class c ON c.relname = i.indexname
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace AND n.nspname = i.schemaname
JOIN pg_index ix ON ix.indexrelid = c.oid
CROSS JOIN LATERAL unnest(ix.indkey) AS k(attnum)
WHERE i.schemaname = 'agenticmcpe_bench_event_stream'
  AND i.tablename = 'event_log'
ORDER BY i.indexname

entries.task_prompt:
I'm staging a small demo for the team on indexing strategies for a bigger clickstream table. Please do this end-to-end in a fresh schema called agenticmcpe_bench_clickstream so nothing leaks elsewhere.

Inside it, create a table page_visits with these columns (all lowercase snake_case): id bigint PRIMARY KEY, region text NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL, response_ms integer NOT NULL, visited_at timestamp NOT NULL. Bulk-seed exactly 5000 rows using a single INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM generate_series(...) statement — please distribute the data realistically across at least four regions (mix of 'us-east', 'us-west', 'eu-west', 'ap-south') and across at least three statuses (mix of 'ok', 'slow', 'error'), and give response_ms a sensible spread (e.g. CASE buckets). After seeding, run ANALYZE on page_visits so the planner has fresh stats.

Then add TWO different indexes on page_visits:
1. A plain btree index on the region column alone.
2. A partial btree index on response_ms with a WHERE clause restricting status = 'slow' (so it only covers the slow subset).

Finally, I want to confirm both indexes exist. First pull the table's structure with the object-details tool so the columns are visible, then run a single SELECT against pg_indexes filtered to this schema and this table that returns each index's name, its full indexdef, and the row indexdef's predicate portion (or expression, when there is one) so I can eyeball the two indexes side-by-side — one plain on region, one partial on response_ms with the status='slow' predicate. The exact total row count of 5000 is important; the per-region and per-status splits are not.

  visited_at timestamp NOT NULL

arguments.sql:
INSERT INTO agenticmcpe_bench_clickstream.page_visits (id, region, status, response_ms, visited_at)
SELECT
  gs                                                                                       AS id,
  CASE (gs % 4)
    WHEN 0 THEN 'us-east'
    WHEN 1 THEN 'us-west'
    WHEN 2 THEN 'eu-west'
    ELSE       'ap-south'
  END                                                                                      AS region,
  CASE (gs % 9)
    WHEN 0 THEN 'error'
    WHEN 1 THEN 'slow'
    WHEN 2 THEN 'slow'
    WHEN 3 THEN 'slow'
    WHEN 4 THEN 'ok'
    WHEN 5 THEN 'ok'
    WHEN 6 THEN 'ok'
    WHEN 7 THEN 'ok'
    ELSE       'ok'
  END                                                                                      AS status,
  CASE (gs % 5)
    WHEN 0 THEN 50 + (gs % 150)
    WHEN 1 THEN 200 + (gs % 300)
    WHEN 2 THEN 600 + (gs % 400)
    WHEN 3 THEN 1200 + (gs % 800)
    ELSE        3000 + (gs % 2000)
  END                                                                                      AS response_ms,
  TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00' + (gs * INTERVAL '1 minute')                              AS visited_at
FROM generate_series(1, 5000) AS gs

post_action_properties.metamorphic: agenticmcpe_bench_clickstream.page_visits holds exactly 5000 rows with regions distributed across us-east/us-west/eu-west/ap-south and statuses distributed across ok/slow/error

I'm hunting planner-estimate drift in the system catalogs and want to focus on pg_class today. Could you do a read-only comparison of how the planner treats a filtered vs. unfiltered projection of pg_class?

Start by listing the schemas in the database so I can see what's here. Then EXPLAIN a projection of (relname, relkind, relnamespace) from pg_class filtered to relkind='r', and EXPLAIN ANALYZE that same filtered projection so I can compare the estimate against the actual row count. After that, EXPLAIN the unfiltered version of the same three columns so I can see how much the estimate grows without the relkind filter.

Once I have those three plans, run a single SELECT that UNION ALLs three COUNT(*)-style legs into one row with columns named 'filtered_estimate_rows', 'unfiltered_estimate_rows', and 'actual_filtered_count' — the first two should be the literal estimate numbers from the EXPLAIN plans above, cast to text, and the third should be the real COUNT(*) for relkind='r', all as text so they line up in a single row. Finally, run a sanity-check SELECT that pairs the literal string 'actual_filtered_count' with the real relkind='r' COUNT(*) on pg_class so the actual figure is independently verifiable.

Everything is read-only — just inspection of the catalogs, no DDL or DML.

entries.task_prompt:
Hi! I'd like to do a read-only pre-deploy extension audit on this Postgres instance. 4. Run a single SELECT against pg_available_extensions filtered to pg_stat_statements so I can see the default_version and the comment that catalog lists for it.

Produce one sanity-check row that places two labeled text columns side-by-side: the literal 'installed_version' next to the extversion currently installed, and the literal 'default_available_version' next to the default_version offered in pg_available_extensions. That way I can eyeball whether an upgrade is available.
6. Run a labeled SELECT that returns 'extension_validity' next to whether pg_stat_statements is marked valid in pg_extension (a simple yes/no-style text label is fine).
7. Run one more labeled SELECT that returns 'index_count_pg_extension' next to the COUNT(*) of rows in pg_extension, so we have a sanity-check total for the inventory.
8. Finally, run the built-in connection-scope health check so we know the audit left the connection in a healthy state.

No DDL, no DML, no writes anywhere — this is a pure read-only inspection.

entries.task_prompt:
Hey, I've got a slow inventory lookup against a prototype stock log and I'd like the index-tuning advisor to recommend the right index for it. Here's the exact setup I'm working with — please follow it step by step.

First, spin up a table called agenticmcpe_bench_inventory_search in the public schema with these columns: id bigint as the primary key, warehouse text, sku text, qty int, is_active boolean, last_stocked timestamptz, and unit_cost_cents int. Then bulk-seed exactly 5000 rows in a single INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM generate_series(1, 5000) statement, distributing warehouse across the four values 'wh_north', 'wh_south', 'wh_east', 'wh_west' and is_active across true/false via CASE, with a deterministic qty (something like ((n * 13) % 250) + 1), a deterministic last_stocked that walks backwards over the last 60 days, and a deterministic unit_cost_cents derived from n with a modulo. Run ANALYZE on the table once the rows are in.

The slow query I care about is this exact lookup, referenced unqualified:
SELECT id, sku, qty
FROM agenticmcpe_bench_inventory_search
WHERE warehouse = 'wh_north'
  AND is_active = true
  AND qty BETWEEN 10 AND 200
ORDER BY last_stocked DESC
LIMIT 40;

Ask the index advisor to analyze that query against the working table, then create the index it recommends, verify the new index shows up for the table via pg_indexes, and finally EXPLAIN the same query so we can see the planner picks it up instead of doing a sequential scan.
entries.task_summary: Create the agenticmcpe_bench_inventory_search table in public with the specified columns, bulk-seed 5000 rows via INSERT ... SELECT FROM generate_series, run ANALYZE, then call the index advisor on the exact slow query (referenced unqualified). Create the recommended index, confirm it appears in pg_indexes for the table, and EXPLAIN the same query to verify the planner uses it instead of a sequential scan.

arguments.sql:
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS public.agenticmcpe_bench_inventory_search (
    id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
    warehouse text,
    sku text,
    qty int,
    is_active boolean,
    last_stocked timestamptz,
    unit_cost_cents int
);

post_action_properties.metamorphic: the table public.agenticmcpe_bench_inventory_search now exists

steps.description: Create the prototype stock log table in the public schema with the required columns and id as the primary key.

arguments.sql:
INSERT INTO public.agenticmcpe_bench_inventory_search (id, warehouse, sku, qty, is_active, last_stocked, unit_cost_cents)
SELECT
    n                                                                AS id,
    CASE (n % 4)
        WHEN 0 THEN 'wh_north'
        WHEN 1 THEN 'wh_south'
        WHEN 2 THEN 'wh_east'
        ELSE      'wh_west'
    END                                                              AS warehouse,
    'sku-' || lpad(n::text, 6, '0')                                  AS sku,
    ((n * 13) % 250) + 1                                             AS qty,
    CASE WHEN n % 2 = 0 THEN true ELSE false END                     AS is_active,
    now() - (((n - 1) % 60) || ' days')::interval                    AS last_stocked,
    (n % 9000) + 100                                                AS unit_cost_cents
FROM generate_series(1, 5000) AS n;

post_action_properties.metamorphic: public.agenticmcpe_bench_inventory_search now holds exactly 5000 rows

steps.description: Bulk-seed exactly 5000 rows in a single INSERT ... SELECT ... entries.task_prompt: Hey, I need a read-only planner-estimate audit on pg_catalog.pg_class. I want to compare what the planner thinks it'll return versus what actually comes back for a simple relname projection. Start by listing the schemas in this database and inventorying what's inside pg_catalog, then peek at pg_class's column metadata so I can see the column types. After that, run four EXPLAIN variants against a relname projection: one estimated plan with a WHERE relkind = 'r' filter, one EXPLAIN ANALYZE of that same filtered query (so I get the actual filtered row count vs. the estimate), one estimated plan with no filter, and one EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the unfiltered query. Then assemble a single UNION ALL SELECT that emits one row of four labeled text values — 'filtered_estimate', 'filtered_actual', 'total_estimate', 'total_actual' — using the literal estimate strings from the EXPLAIN outputs for the estimate columns and real COUNT(*) casts to text for the actual counts (filtered with the WHERE relkind = 'r' clause, total without it). Follow that with a labeled sanity-check SELECT that pairs the literal label 'filtered_actual' with the real filtered COUNT(*) cast to text. Finish off with the built-in connection-scope health check. The whole thing should be pure reads — nothing gets created, modified, or deleted.

thinking: I need to orient myself in this unfamiliar database. First I'll list all schemas to see what exists.
Then I'll inventory the objects inside information_schema to see what views/tables are available there for metadata queries.
Next I'll inventory the objects in pg_catalog so I know which system tables are reachable.
I'll drill into detailed column metadata for information_schema.columns — that view is critical for inspecting user table columns.
I'll also pull detailed column metadata for pg_catalog.pg_class so I can understand the core catalog.
Now run three EXPLAIN variants against pg_class — a filtered projection (relkind='r'), the same with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and an unfiltered projection — to capture planner estimates vs actuals.
Then run three EXPLAIN variants against information_schema.tables for table_type='BASE TABLE' (filtered estimated, filtered ANALYZE'd, unfiltered estimated).

Now issue a single UNION ALL labeled-count report that emits one row of labeled text columns combining the literal EXPLAIN estimate strings with real COUNT(*) casts for filtered vs total rows on pg_class.
Follow that with a labeled sanity-check SELECT that pairs 'filtered_actual' with the real COUNT(*) for relkind='r' cast to text.
Then a second labeled sanity-check SELECT pairing 'tables_base_total' with the real COUNT(*) for table_type='BASE TABLE' in information_schema.tables cast to text.
Close with the built-in connection-scope health check via analyze_db_health. Every step is pure read-only — no DDL/DML.

Hey, I'm spinning up a tiny audit table for API tokens we hand out internally, and I'd like to test the workflow of adding a typed column to a table that already has data in it. Can you do this end to end inside a dedicated schema called agenticmcpe_bench_api_tokens (please don't touch public or anything else)?

Inside that schema, create a table called api_tokens with these columns and types: id serial PRIMARY KEY, token_label text NOT NULL, issued_to text, created_on date NOT NULL. Then insert exactly these five rows, in this order: (1, 'svc-orders', 'orders-team', '2024-04-01'), (2, 'svc-billing', 'billing-team', '2024-04-02'), (3, 'svc-search', 'search-team', '2024-04-03'), (4, 'svc-archive', 'data-team', '2024-04-04'), (5, 'svc-metrics', 'platform-team', '2024-04-05).

Backfill it in two UPDATEs: first set status = 'active' for the row where token_label = 'svc-orders', then in a single UPDATE set status = 'rotated' for the remaining rows (so a WHERE clause that covers the other four token_labels). 

Finish by reading the evolved shape back as a projection of id, token_label, status ordered by id, and also pull the table's full structure so I can confirm the new column is there with the right type.

Hey, I'm tuning a tiny stop-lookup query and want to confirm a btree index actually gets created on the right column. Please do this end to end inside a dedicated schema called agenticmcpe_bench_route_lookup — don't touch public or any other schema.

Inside that schema, create a table called route_stops with these columns and types: id serial PRIMARY KEY, route_code text NOT NULL, stop_sequence integer NOT NULL, station_name text NOT NULL, arrived_at timestamp NOT NULL, rider_count integer NOT NULL. Hey, could you do me a small read-only planner audit before I poke at production? I'd like you to walk me from the top down: first show me what schemas exist, then inventory what's inside pg_catalog and inside information_schema so I can confirm pg_class and information_schema.tables are both reachable. After that, give me the detailed column listings of pg_catalog.pg_class and information_schema.tables so I can see exactly which columns I'm filtering on.

Once that's done, please run a few EXPLAINs for me on pg_class — one estimated plan filtered to relname = 'pg_class' projecting relname, relkind, relpages; one EXPLAIN ANALYZE of the same filtered query so I can see the real row count; and one estimated unfiltered plan projecting the same three columns with no WHERE so I can compare planner estimates. Then do one more estimated EXPLAIN against information_schema.tables filtered to table_type = 'BASE TABLE' projecting table_schema and table_name, just so I can see how that catalog plans.

Finally, run two labeled sanity-check SELECTs: one that pairs the literal label 'filtered_actual_pg_class' with the real COUNT(*) of pg_class rows matching relname = 'pg_class' cast to text, and one that pairs 'unfiltered_actual_pg_class' with the real COUNT(*) of pg_class cast to text. And wrap it up with the standard connection-scope health check. Everything should stay strictly read-only — no DDL or DML at any point.

entries.task_prompt:
Hey, I'm prepping for a small schema change later this week and I'd like a strictly read-only health snapshot of the Postgres instance before I touch anything. Could you walk me through it step by step?

Start by listing all the schemas so I can confirm information_schema and pg_catalog are both present. Then inventory what's inside pg_catalog and what's inside information_schema so I have a feel for what we're working with. After that, pull the detailed column listings for pg_catalog.pg_class and information_schema.tables — I want to see exactly which columns we'd be projecting or filtering on.

Once the catalog is mapped, run three built-in health checks for me: the connection-scope one, the vacuum-scope one, and the index-scope one. I want to know if anything is already flagged (long-running connections, tables that need vacuuming, invalid/unused indexes) before I start changing things.

Then run three small labeled sanity-check SELECTs, each one row, all cast to text:
- one that pairs the literal label 'pg_class_total_rows' with the real COUNT(*) of pg_catalog.pg_class,
- one that pairs the literal label 'pg_class_estimated_row_estimate' with the planner's stored reltuples estimate for pg_class (pull it directly from pg_class so I can see the estimate vs. the real count side by side),
- and one that pairs the literal label 'current_setting_search_path' with current_setting('search_path').

Finally, close it out with the buffer-scope health check so I can see cache-hit context in the final report. Everything stays strictly read-only — only SELECTs, catalog inspections, and the built-in health checks. No DDL or DML at any point.

Set up a product_catalog table with some real guardrails so junk data can't slip in later. Do the whole thing inside a fresh schema called agenticmcpe_bench_constraint_shield — don't touch any other schema.

Inside that schema, create a table called product_catalog with these columns:
- id: serial, primary key
- sku: text, not null, unique
- product_name: text, not null
- category: text, not null
- unit_price: numeric(10,2)
- stock_qty: integer
- is_active: boolean, not null, default true

And add these constraints:
- category must be one of 'Electronics', 'Apparel', 'Home', 'Food' (CHECK constraint)
- unit_price must be >= 0 (CHECK constraint)
- stock_qty must be >= 0 (CHECK constraint)

Then seed it with exactly these six rows, in this exact order:

1, SKU-001, Wireless Mouse, Electronics, 24.99, 150, true
2, SKU-002, Cotton T-Shirt, Apparel, 15.50, 300, true
3, SKU-003, Ceramic Mug, Home, 8.75, 80, true
4, SKU-004, USB Hub, Electronics, 32.00, 0, true
5, SKU-005, Granola Bar, Food, 2.49, 500, true
6, SKU-006, Wool Socks, Apparel, 11.00, 200, false

Once the rows are in, please verify by:
- running a SELECT that returns id, sku, product_name, category, unit_price from product_catalog ordered by id,
- a single-row labeled SELECT that pairs the literal label 'total_products' with COUNT(*) of the table cast to text,
- a single-row labeled SELECT that pairs the literal label 'active_products' with COUNT(*) of rows where is_active = true cast to text,
- a single-row labeled SELECT that pairs the literal label 'electronics_count' with COUNT(*) of rows where category = 'Electronics' cast to text,
- a single-row labeled SELECT that pairs the literal label 'low_stock_count' with COUNT(*) of rows where stock_qty = 0 cast to text,
- and inspect the detailed structure of product_catalog so I can see all the constraints listed.

Finally, also pull a SELECT against pg_constraint for the product_catalog table that returns conname, contype, and pg_get_constraintdef(oid) cast to text, ordered by conname, so I have a hard list of every constraint that actually got created. Everything stays inside agenticmcpe_bench_constraint_shield.

Inside that schema, build a `customer_orders` table with columns id serial PRIMARY KEY, order_code text, customer_name text, item_sku text, and qty int. Please deliberately do NOT add any unique constraint on order_code — duplicates on that business key must be allowed so we can clean them up.

('ORD-001', 'alice', 'widget-A', 2),
('ORD-001', 'alice', 'widget-A', 2),
('ORD-002', 'bob',   'widget-B', 1),

Everything stays inside `agenticmcpe_bench_dedup_orders` — please don't touch public or any other schema.

Hey, I'm stress-testing an indexing strategy on a synthetic event-log table and I'd like your help running the whole thing end-to-end against a fresh dedicated schema — nothing in public or any other schema should be touched. The schema is `agenticmcpe_bench_event_log` (snake_case, please use it exactly).

Inside that schema, please build an `event_log` table with these columns: `id` bigint NOT NULL, `event_code` text NOT NULL, `payload` jsonb NOT NULL, and `created_at` timestamptz NOT NULL. No primary key, no defaults tied to the clock — I'll seed a literal timestamp myself.

Then bulk-seed exactly 3000 rows in a single INSERT ... SELECT FROM generate_series statement. I'd like `id` to come straight from generate_series(1, 3000), `event_code` to rotate through a small fixed set of codes (e.g. 'login', 'logout', 'purchase', 'error') so each code appears roughly equally, `payload` to be a small jsonb object like `{"severity": "info", "source": "web"}` with severity varying between 'info', 'warn', and 'error' so we have a meaningful subset for the partial index, and `created_at` to be the literal timestamp `'2025-01-15 12:00:00+00'` so verification is stable. The only promise I care about is the total row count being exactly 3000 — please don't promise any specific per-code or per-severity breakdown.

After seeding, please run ANALYZE on `event_log` so planner stats are fresh. Then inspect the table's detailed structure so I can see the column types.

Now for the indexing itself: create TWO different indexes on `event_log`. First, a plain btree index on `event_code`. Second, a partial btree index on `payload` restricted to rows where `payload->>'severity' = 'error'` — that's the 'variant' part I want to confirm. After creating both, read back the index definitions for `event_log` from `pg_indexes` ordered by `indexname` ASC so I can see the exact CREATE INDEX statements for both. Finish with a single labeled SELECT that pairs the literal `'index_count'` with the actual count of indexes on `event_log` cast to text, just as a hard sanity check.

Everything stays inside `agenticmcpe_bench_event_log` — public and other schemas must remain untouched.

Step 2: list_objects on pg_catalog to find candidate catalog tables for the EXPLAIN drill.
Step 3: get_object_details on pg_class to confirm the column layout (relname, relkind, relnamespace, etc.) before writing the EXPLAIN queries.
Step 4: explain_query on an unfiltered SELECT COUNT(*) FROM pg_catalog.pg_class — get the planner estimate without actually running.
Step 5: explain_query on the same unfiltered count but with ANALYZE — gets the actual row count and true timing.
Step 6: explain_query on a filtered variant, COUNT(*) FROM pg_catalog.pg_class WHERE relkind = 'r' — see the estimate for the regular-table subset.
Step 7: explain_query again with ANALYZE on that filtered variant — get the real count for relkind='r'.
Step 8: execute_sql a labeled sanity-check SELECT that pairs the literal 'actual_pg_class_rows' with COUNT(*) cast to text so the analyst has a real number to compare against the EXPLAIN estimates.
Step 9: analyze_db_health with a connection-scope check to wrap things up.

entries.task_prompt: Hey, I just got pointed at this Postgres instance and I'd like a quick read-only orientation tour before I touch anything. Could you list out all the schemas that are here, then take me through what's in information_schema and pg_catalog so I can see the catalog tables and views I'm working with? After that, pull the column metadata for information_schema.tables, pg_namespace, pg_class, and pg_attribute — I want to know what fields are actually exposed on each of them. Once those layouts are in front of me, run two labeled sanity-check SELECTs that pair a literal label with the row count cast to text — one for the number of rows in information_schema.tables and one for the number of rows in pg_catalog.pg_class. Wrap it up with a connection-scope database health check so I know the connection pool is healthy. Everything should stay strictly read-only — SELECTs against the system catalogs plus the standard health inspection, no DDL or DML.
entries.task_summary: A strictly read-only orientation tour of the Postgres instance: list all schemas, enumerate objects in information_schema and pg_catalog, pull column metadata for information_schema.tables, pg_namespace, pg_class, and pg_attribute, then run two labeled SELECTs that cast row counts to text and finish with a connection-scope database health check. Only read-only tools (list_schemas, list_objects, get_object_details, execute_sql for SELECTs, analyze_db_health) are used; no DDL/DML.

entries.task_prompt: I'm a DBA doing a read-only first look at a Postgres instance I haven't seen before, and I want a single coherent snapshot of what the catalog actually exposes. Could you walk me through it step by step? Start by listing the schemas that are visible, then inventory the objects sitting inside pg_catalog and inside information_schema so I can see the catalog tables and views I'm dealing with. After that, pull the detailed column metadata for information_schema.tables, information_schema.columns, pg_class, and pg_namespace — I want to know what fields each one exposes before I query them. Once those layouts are in front of me, run a few labeled sanity-check SELECTs that pair a literal label with a value cast to text: one for the current database, one for the current user, one for the server version, one for the count of distinct user (non-system) schemas that actually contain tables, one for the total estimated row count across all user tables (sum of pg_class.reltuples joined to pg_namespace and filtered away from pg_catalog / information_schema), and one for how many rows pg_settings holds. Finish with a connection-scope database health check so I know the connection itself is healthy. Please stay strictly read-only the whole way — SELECTs against the system catalogs and the standard health inspection, no DDL or DML.
entries.task_summary: Read-only first-look snapshot of a Postgres instance: list schemas, inventory objects inside pg_catalog and information_schema, pull column metadata for four system-catalog/information-schema objects (information_schema.tables, information_schema.columns, pg_class, pg_namespace), run six labeled SELECTs pairing a literal with a cast value (current_database, current_user, server version, count of user schemas containing tables, total estimated row count across user tables, pg_settings row count), then run a connection health check via analyze_db_health. No DDL or DML anywhere — all reads.

entries.task_prompt: I'm a new team member trying to get my bearings on the Postgres instance before any real work begins, and I want to understand how the planner behaves on simple system-catalog queries. Please walk me through this read-only review: start by listing every schema in the database, then inventory the objects inside pg_catalog so I can see the system tables available. Pull the column metadata for pg_catalog.pg_class and information_schema.tables so I know what to filter on. After that, show me the EXPLAIN plan for a plain unfiltered COUNT(*) over pg_class, then a second EXPLAIN plan for a filtered count where relkind = 'r' so I can see how the planner changes with a predicate. Run a labeled SELECT that pairs the literal 'pg_class_relkind_r_rows' with the actual cast count under that same filter so I can sanity-check the plan. Then produce an EXPLAIN ANALYZE for a join that pairs pg_class with information_schema.tables using table_schema = 'pg_catalog' and relkind = 'r', and follow it with a second labeled SELECT pairing the literal 'user_table_count' with a cast count of tables whose schema is neither pg_catalog nor information_schema. Finish with a connection-scope database health check. Everything must be strictly read-only — no DDL, no DML, no changes to public or any other schema.
entries.task_summary: A purely read-only onboarding review of the Postgres instance: discover schemas, inventory pg_catalog objects, fetch column metadata for pg_class and information_schema.tables, run EXPLAIN plans for unfiltered and filtered COUNT(*) on pg_class, run a labeled SELECT to verify the filtered count, run EXPLAIN ANALYZE for a join of pg_class with information_schema.tables (filtered to pg_catalog tables that are ordinary relations), run a labeled SELECT for the user-table count, and finish with a connection-scope database health check. No DDL or DML is executed.

entries.task_prompt: I'm a DBA about to take over an unfamiliar Postgres instance before a production release and I need a strictly read-only health audit. List every schema in the database, then inventory the objects in pg_catalog and the public schema so I can see what we're dealing with. Pull the column metadata for pg_stat_user_tables so I know what fields the per-table stats view exposes. Run the database health checks in this order: connection, vacuum, buffer, index, and sequence. Also run a labeled sanity-check SELECT that pairs the literal 'pg_stat_user_tables_rows' with the cast count of rows currently in pg_stat_user_tables, and a labeled environment-identity SELECT that pairs the literals 'database', 'current_user', and 'server_version' with current_database(), current_user, and version()::text respectively. Finally, fetch the column metadata for pg_settings so I can later look at runtime knobs. Every step is read-only — no DDL, no DML, no changes to public or any other schema.
entries.task_summary: Performs a strictly read-only health audit of the Postgres instance: lists all schemas, inventories objects in pg_catalog and public, fetches column metadata for pg_stat_user_tables and pg_settings, runs the connection/vacuum/buffer/index/sequence health checks in order, and runs two labeled sanity/identity SELECTs that pair literal labels with live values via current_database(), current_user, version()::text and a cast count from pg_stat_user_tables.

steps.description: Enumerate every schema in the database so the DBA can see all namespaces present, including pg_catalog and public.
Inventory the objects (tables, views, sequences, extensions) living in pg_catalog so the DBA knows what system objects are present.
Inventory the objects in the public schema to see what user-defined objects exist before the production release.
Pull column metadata (and any constraints/indexes) for pg_stat_user_tables so the DBA knows exactly which per-table stats fields are exposed.
Run the connection health check first to surface active sessions, limits and connection-related issues.
Run the vacuum health check second to flag tables with dead tuples, missed autovacuum runs and transaction-id wraparound risk.
Run the buffer cache health check third to see hit ratios, top consumers and buffer-related pressure.
Run the index health check fourth to flag invalid, unused or bloated indexes.
Run the sequence health check last to inspect sequence exhaustion risk and current usage.

entries.task_prompt: Performance-tuned engineer here with a slow lookup I need to fix. Set up a working table called agenticmcpe_bench_order_search in the public schema with columns id bigint, customer_email text, status text, region text, total_cents int, and created_at timestamptz — no primary key, no indexes. Bulk-seed it with exactly 3000 rows via a single INSERT ... SELECT FROM generate_series(...) statement, rotating customer_email across a small handful of literal addresses, status across literal values like 'open', 'closed', 'pending', and 'review', region across literal values like 'us-east', 'us-west', 'eu-west', and 'ap-south', total_cents across a small range of literal integers, and a single literal fixed timestamp for created_at. Run ANALYZE on the table, then verify the exact row count is 3000 with a labeled sanity SELECT. After that, run two concrete lookup queries against the table — referenced UNQUALIFIED (no schema prefix) — one filtering where customer_email equals a literal address and one filtering where status equals a literal value. Hand those two queries to the index advisor and let it recommend indexes. Create the highest-impact index it recommends on the table, re-run ANALYZE, then confirm by querying pg_indexes that the new index exists and by EXPLAINing one of the lookups that the plan now uses an Index Scan rather than a Seq Scan on that table.

entries.task_prompt: I'm doing a pre-deploy disk-and-buffer review on this Postgres instance and I want to figure out what is actually taking up space. Start by listing all the schemas so I know the lay of the land, then enumerate the objects inside pg_catalog and pull the column metadata for pg_class so I know what I can filter on. After that, run a labeled SELECT that joins pg_class to pg_namespace and reports the top 10 largest relations overall using pg_total_relation_size and pg_size_pretty, restricted to relkind in ('r','i','t','m'). Follow it with a second labeled SELECT on pg_class for ordinary tables only (relkind = 'r') using pg_total_relation_size / pg_size_pretty, also top 10. Then run a labeled SELECT that reports, as the literal 'tables_with_toast', the COUNT(*) of ordinary tables that have a non-zero pg_class.reltoastrelid. Next, run a labeled SELECT against pg_statio_user_tables that pairs each table name with pg_size_pretty(heap_blks_read + idx_blks_read + toast_blks_read), ordered descending and limited to 5 — I want to see whether the physically largest relations match the ones churning the buffer cache. Finish with two health checks: first the buffer check, then the index check. Everything is read-only — no DDL or DML anywhere.
entries.task_summary: Read-only review: list schemas, enumerate pg_catalog objects, pull pg_class columns, then run four labeled SELECTs against pg_class/pg_namespace/pg_statio_user_tables to size relations and toast usage. Finish with buffer and index health checks.

arguments.sql:
SELECT c.relname AS relation_name,
       n.nspname AS schema_name,
       c.relkind AS relkind,
       pg_total_relation_size(c.oid) AS total_bytes,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_total_relation_size(c.oid)) AS total_pretty
FROM pg_class AS c
JOIN pg_namespace AS n ON n.oid = c.relnamespace
WHERE c.relkind IN ('r','i','t','m')
ORDER BY pg_total_relation_size(c.oid) DESC
LIMIT 10

WHERE c.relkind = 'r'

entries.task_prompt: Hey, I'm an SRE and I want to do a quick vac-stats review and figure out whether autovacuum is actually keeping up on this Postgres instance — I've been noticing some sluggishness and I'd like to see it in numbers before I escalate. Could you walk me through it? Start by listing all the schemas so I can see what user tables we're talking about, then pick a user schema (your call, just one that's likely to have activity) and list its tables so I know what's in scope. After that, run the dedicated vacuum health check so I have the overall verdict. Then I want a labeled SELECT against pg_stat_user_tables that pairs each literal column name ('relname', 'n_live_tup', 'n_dead_tup', 'last_autovacuum', 'last_autoanalyze') with the matching column cast to text (use ::text on the timestamp columns and on the counts), ordered by n_dead_tup descending, limited to 10 rows — that's the main table I want to look at. Follow it with a second labeled SELECT on the same view pairing 'vacuum_count', 'autovacuum_count', 'analyze_count', 'autoanalyze_count' all cast to text, ordered by n_dead_tup desc, limit 10 — I want to confirm autovacuum has actually been firing. Next, a labeled SELECT that pairs the literal 'autovacuum_on' with the current ::text value of the autovacuum setting, and another labeled SELECT pairing 'autovacuum_naptime' with the current ::text value of the autovacuum_naptime setting — I want to confirm autovacuum is enabled and see how often it wakes up. One more labeled SELECT please: pair the literal 'dead_ratio' with (n_dead_tup::text || '/' || n_live_tup::text) for each row ordered by n_dead_tup desc, limit 10 — that gives me a quick feel for the pressure. And one more labeled SELECT that pairs the literal 'flagged_tables' with relname (cast to text) for the actual table names currently flagged, ordered by n_dead_tup desc, limit 10. Finish with a full connection-scope database health check. Everything's read-only — don't run any DDL or DML, just inspect the catalogs.

entries.task_prompt:
Hey — I'm new on the team and I'd like to do a read-only privilege review of this Postgres instance so I can understand who can do what before I start asking for grants. Could you walk me through it using only inspection tools? No DDL or DML of any kind, please.

To start, list every schema in the database so I can see the landscape. Then enumerate the objects that live inside information_schema and inside pg_catalog, so I know which system views I'm about to touch. After that, pull the column metadata for information_schema.role_table_grants and for pg_catalog.pg_roles so I can see the exact column names and types I'll be querying.

Once I have the lay of the land, run a labeled SELECT that pairs the literal string 'role_count' with COUNT(*) over pg_roles — just a single number for how many roles exist on this instance. Then run a bounded SELECT with LIMIT 10 over information_schema.role_table_grants restricted to tables whose table_schema is 'information_schema', ordered by grantee, table_name, and privilege_type, so I can eyeball which roles have which privileges on the system catalog's own tables.

Next, give me the first 10 rows from pg_roles ordered by oid ascending, with rolname and rolsuper both cast to text and paired with the literal labels 'rolname' and 'rolsuper' for readability. After that, run an identity SELECT that pairs the literal 'current_session_user' with current_user::text and 'current_session_role' with session_user::text, so I can confirm who I'm running as while doing this review. Then run one more labeled SELECT that pairs the literal 'distinct_grantees' with COUNT(DISTINCT grantee)::text over the same information_schema.role_table_grants sample, so I know how many unique grantees actually show up in that grant list.

Finish with a connection-scope database health check so the privilege review ends on a clean health signal. Everything stays read-only — don't create, modify, or drop anything, and don't query user tables. Just system catalogs and session info.
entries.task_summary: A read-only privilege review walkthrough. The sequence lists schemas, enumerates objects in information_schema and pg_catalog, fetches column details for information_schema.role_table_grants and pg_catalog.pg_roles, then runs a series of labeled, bounded SELECTs against system catalogs only (pg_roles, information_schema.role_table_grants restricted to information_schema tables, current_user/session_user). entries.task_prompt:
Hey — I'm onboarding onto the team and I'd like to do a read-only vacuum/autovacuum health review on this Postgres instance so I can tell whether autovacuum is actually keeping up before we start onboarding new write-heavy workloads. Could you walk me through it using only inspection tools, no DDL or DML of any kind?

To start, list every schema in the database so I can see the landscape. Then enumerate the objects inside pg_catalog so I know which statistics views are available before I start querying them. After that, pull the column metadata for pg_stat_user_tables and for pg_settings so I can see the exact column names and types I'll be querying against.

Once I have the lay of the land, run a labeled SELECT against pg_stat_user_tables that pairs 'table_name' with relname::text, 'live_tuples' with n_live_tup::text, 'dead_tuples' with n_dead_tup::text, and 'dead_pct' with a CASE expression that computes the dead-tuple ratio as text (handling the zero-live-tuple case), ordered by n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 10 — I want to see dead-tuple pressure per table. Then run a second labeled SELECT that pairs 'total_live_tuples' with SUM(n_live_tup)::text and 'total_dead_tuples' with SUM(n_dead_tup)::text over pg_stat_user_tables, so I get an instance-wide aggregate.

Next, give me a labeled SELECT that surfaces autovacuum firing activity — pairing 'table_name' with relname::text, 'av_count' with autovacuum_count::text, 'aa_count' with autoanalyze_count::text, 'last_autovacuum' with last_autovacuum::text, and 'last_autoanalyze' with last_autoanalyze::text, all from pg_stat_user_tables, ordered by autovacuum_count DESC LIMIT 10. After that, run a labeled SELECT over pg_settings that pairs 'setting_name' with name::text and 'setting_value' with setting::text, filtered to the names autovacuum, autovacuum_naptime, autovacuum_max_workers, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold, autovacuum_analyze_threshold, and track_counts, ordered by name, so I can see the live autovacuum configuration.

Then run one more labeled SELECT that pairs 'tables_with_dead_tuples' with COUNT(*)::text filtered to n_dead_tup > 0 and 'tables_never_autovacuumed' with COUNT(*)::text filtered to autovacuum_count = 0, both from pg_stat_user_tables, so I can quantify how widespread the dead-tuple pressure actually is across the instance. Finish with a connection-scope database health check that includes the vacuum health check so the review ends on a clean health signal. Everything stays read-only — don't create, modify, or drop anything, and don't query user tables. Just system catalogs and session info.
entries.task_summary: Read-only autovacuum health review. We first map the landscape by listing all schemas, enumerating objects in pg_catalog to discover available statistics views, and pulling column metadata for pg_stat_user_tables and pg_settings so we use correct column names. We then run a series of labeled SELECTs against pg_stat_user_tables to expose per-table dead-tuple pressure (dead_pct with zero-live-tuple handling), instance-wide live/dead aggregates, autovacuum/autoanalyze activity, and counts of tables with dead tuples and tables never autovacuumed. We also SELECT the live autovacuum GUC settings from pg_settings. Finally we run a connection-scope database health check with the vacuum check included. All steps are pure inspections of system catalogs — no DDL/DML and no user-table access.

entries.task_prompt: Hey, before I push the next deploy I'd like a quick read-only pass on autovacuum health on this Postgres instance — nothing more. Could you start by listing every schema so I can see what user schemas are in play, then enumerate the objects in pg_catalog to confirm the right statistics views are available, and pull column metadata for pg_stat_user_tables and pg_settings so we don't guess any column names. After that, run a series of labeled SELECTs against the system catalogs only (no user tables touched): (1) the top 10 rows from pg_stat_user_tables ordered by dead-tuple percentage desc, showing schemaname, relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_autovacuum::text, last_autoanalyze::text and a dead_pct that gracefully handles zero-live-tuple rows, paired with the literal label 'top_dead_tuple_pressure'; (2) instance-wide aggregates SUM(n_live_tup)::text and SUM(n_dead_tup)::text, paired with the literal labels 'instance_live_tuples' and 'instance_dead_tuples'; (3) counts of tables with dead tuples and tables that have never been autovacuumed, paired with the literal labels 'tables_with_dead_tuples' and 'tables_never_autovacuumed'; and (4) the live autovacuum GUC settings from pg_settings (autovacuum, autovacuum_naptime, autovacuum_max_workers, autovacuum_vacuum_threshold, autovacuum_analyze_threshold) paired with the literal label 'autovacuum_settings'. Then run the vacuum health check via the database health tool, and finish with a full connection-scope database health check. No DDL, no DML, only system-catalog reads — every SELECT must pair its output with a text literal label so it's unambiguous.

entries.task_prompt: Hey, I'm prototyping a small reporting layer and I'd love to play with a materialized view end-to-end so the dashboard hits a precomputed summary instead of re-aggregating raw rows on every refresh. Could you carve out a fresh sandbox schema called `agenticmcpe_bench_mv_signuplab` and wire the whole thing up for me? Inside it, create a base table `daily_signups` with columns `id` (PK), `signup_date` (date), `country` (text), and `plan` (text). Seed it with eight verbatim rows spread across a couple of dates, countries, and plans. Then define a materialized view `daily_signups_summary` that aggregates by `signup_date` — I want the order count, distinct country count, and distinct plan count per day, paired with the text literal label `per_day_summary` so the output is unambiguous. Before we disturb anything, run a labeled SELECT * FROM the materialized view ordered by signup_date so I can see the precomputed totals. Next, slip one extra row into `daily_signups` so the materialized view goes stale, then REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW so the precomputed totals are current again. After the refresh, give me three labeled SELECTs: (1) the refreshed per-day breakdown ordered by signup_date, (2) a labeled SUM of the order count across the whole view paired with the literal label `refreshed_grand_total_orders`, and (3) a sanity-check SELECT that pairs the literal label `new_row_visible` with the count of rows matching the newly inserted (signup_date, country). Wrap it up with a connection-scope database health check. Please keep every single write inside `agenticmcpe_bench_mv_signuplab` — nothing should leak into public.

entries.task_prompt:
I'm prepping for a Postgres privilege review and want to walk through the system catalogs without touching any user data. Start by listing every schema on the instance so I can see what's installed. Then enumerate the objects inside information_schema and pg_catalog so I can locate the privilege views and the roles catalog. After that, pull the column metadata for information_schema.role_table_grants and pg_catalog.pg_roles so I'm certain about the column names before quoting them in queries.

With the metadata confirmed, run a labeled SELECT that pairs the literal 'role_count' with COUNT(*) from pg_catalog.pg_roles. Then run a bounded SELECT (LIMIT 10, ordered by grantee, table_name, privilege_type) against information_schema.role_table_grants restricted to tables that actually live in the information_schema schema — that bounded slice is what I want to audit. Pair a separate labeled SELECT with the literal 'distinct_grantees' and COUNT(DISTINCT grantee)::text from that same information_schema grants sample so I can see how many distinct grantees exist on the system schema.

I also want to know who I'm connected as: emit a labeled identity SELECT pairing 'current_session_user' with current_user::text and 'current_session_role' with session_user::text. And pull the first 10 rows from pg_roles ordered by oid, with rolname and rolsuper cast to text and paired with literal labels so I can spot superusers at a glance.

Wrap the whole walkthrough up with a connection-scope database health check. Everything stays read-only — no DDL, no DML, no user tables.
